As for your question, humans have been aware of the existence of outer space for thousands of years. The earliest recorded observations of the night sky date back to ancient civilizations in Mesopotamia, Egypt, and Greece around 4000-5000 years ago. These early cultures recognized the stars and constellations, and some even believed in a flat Earth with a dome above it.

The concept of a void of darkness in space, illuminated only by stars and galaxies, developed over time through the work of ancient Greek philosophers such as Aristotle and Eratosthenes. They proposed that the Earth was a sphere and that the stars and planets were distant objects that could not be seen from the surface.

The idea that space was blue like the morning sky was a common misconception in the 17th and 18th centuries. This notion was based on the idea that the Earth was surrounded by a "blue sphere" that reflected the color of the sky. However, this idea was later disproven by scientists such as Isaac Newton and James Bradley, who demonstrated that the color of the sky is due to the scattering of sunlight by the atmosphere, not the color of the space itself.

The modern understanding of outer space as a vast, dark void was developed in the 19th and 20th centuries through the work of astronomers such as William Herschel, Edwin Hubble, and Carl Sagan. They used telescopes and other instruments to study the stars, galaxies, and other celestial objects, and their discoveries revolutionized our understanding of the universe.
